What knowledge has the government or the minister as to the ability of the bank to employ advantageously this additional capital? Obviously it is not asked for by the bank; it is unnecessary for it to have the additional capital to carry on its business. The general view was that the government proposed, in the light of the statements made by the Prime Minister when in opposition, and by others, to acquire the outstanding capital stock of the bank, $5,000,000. This creation of an additional $5,100,000 doubles the capital of the bank. There has been no suggestion that there was any shortage, of the capital necessary to enable the bank to carry on its business.
I should like to ask the minister on what basis he found it desirable to increase the

Bank of Canada
capital of this institution in order to attain the ends he has in view. I cannot but think that the general conception of what was meant by the statements made was that the bank's capital of 85,000,000 was to be taken over by the crown. Of course many people believed that the bank was to be a publicly operated institution, run as a department of government, and would be available for the discount of bills and for public credit for all those who desired to do business with it. That is the conception which many people formed, in opposition to the views expressed by ourselves at that time. The important thing is, on what basis does the government suggest that it was desirable to have another 85,100,000 capital for this institution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
The answer is very
simple. To justify control by the government majority, and the appointment by the government of the majority of the board of directors, it was deemed desirable that a majority of the capital stock should be acquired by the government.

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
The minister will at once admit that it is competent for the bill to provide that out of the seven directors to be elected four shall be named by the government, and that the shareholders elect only three. There was never any difficulty about that. For instance it is provided at the moment that the Deputy Minister of Finance shall sit on the board but not vote; the governor is not a director, neither is the deputy governor, but he becomes a member of the board. There never has been any difficulty with respect to this parliament by appropriate action providing that the governor in council may appoint four directors out of the seven. It was not necessary to increase the capital stock to accomplish that end. The power of parliament to take that action is unquestioned, and is best evidenced by the fact that the governor and deputy governor are members of the board but not directors of the bank. All that is necessary is to provide that four persons be named by the government to be directors of the institution. To double the capital stock and add $100,000 more to accomplish that strikes me as a very strange anomaly, because it is provided that these same people, holding 85,100,000 worth of stock, cannot vote at shareholders' meetings for the election of directors. The capital stock is now $10,100,000 and only $5,000,000 can vote to elect directors. The other $5,100,000 must remain silent and not vote, because the government proposes to appoint four directors with eight votes. If that is not putting the cart before the horse, I cannot understand the ordinary significance
of a transaction of this kind. Here it is provided that you double the capital of the bank and then add another $100,000, and the minister says that doing that will give the government control of the directors. The government does not propose to acquire the outstanding capital stock, as they have a right to do, in the same way as they would acquire a piece of land or any other commodity they might wish to possess-either by appropriation proceedings, by arbitrations or by reference to the exchequer court to fix the value and take them over. No; to accomplish the desired end the government has said: "We are going to increase the capital stock by doubling it and adding $100,000 more to it, and then we will not give them a vote." These four directors need not be men who possess the qualifications of holders of class "A" shares; they are merely named without any powers, and the government has no power to participate in the election of the three that are to be elected. I must confess I do not understand it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
There is in Canada what is known as the consolidated revenue fund, which, by law, represents all the money going into the treasury, from whatever source. In this instance we have an investment which

will yield a certain return. The provision at page 5 of the bill indicates that the minister may pay for the shares acquired out of the consolidated revenue fund. That increases the dominion's investment account by that amount of money. It is not merely a bookkeeping entry; it is an investment, and one which will yield more than or at least as much as the money costs. I cannot tell my hon. friend precisely what will be the cost of any particular sum of money out of the consolidated revenue fund. I cannot do that, because the borrowing operations of the government cover a great variety of requirements at a great variety of periods. At the present time, for instance, there are outstanding something like $120,000,000 of three months treasury bills, in respect of which the effective rate is below one per cent per annum, but there are also outstanding issues of securities with varying terms. If my hon. friend were to ask me what rate I would be paying and what terms I would be offering two or three months from now I could not tell him; I would have to endeavour to make the best possible arrangement under the financial conditions then prevailing, which might be more favourable to short term and less favourable to long term, or the reverse of that. Matters of this kind require continuous close attention, study and determination in the light of circumstances prevailing at the time money is secured to replenish the consolidated revenue fund.

speechtext:
I am addressing the Chair. There are no such tactics as those assumed by the minister. I am desirous of obtaining information, and that information I propose to get. Here is a bank created by the parliament of Canada, with a capital of $5,000,000. It pays 4J per cent on that investment. Its capital is being doubled now, without any request from the bank or suggestion that it found itself short of capital, and the minister said that the reason for it was the desire to obtain control for the government of the institution. Instead of proceeding to expropriate the shares, as he has the right to do, and as normally would be done, by taking the proper steps to expropriate $5,000,000 of shares, and have their value fixed by the exchequer court or by arbitration, the minister increased the capital of the bank by $5,100,000, making the total capital $10,100,000, and the statute says that the money necessary to pay for them shall be paid out of corn-solidated revenue. It does not leave it a question of option, but says they "shall" be paid for out of the consolidated revenue fund. We know from the statement made by the finance minister on the budget that this country has made no provision for that payment. Therefore the money must be borrowed, and the very proper question was asked, whether or not it would be borrowed. To that question the minister replied that if we had to pay it now we would not have to borrow, which means that there is $5,000,000 in the treasury that might be used for that purpose. That was no answer to the question. The question was, will this money have to be borrowed? The minister clothed [DOT]his answer in many words, as to its being an investment. It is an investment in the bank, and according to the statement made by the minister on the budget-and certainly the revenues of the country so far
as customs are concerned have not increased beyond his expectations-the money will have to be borrowed.
The point I was endeavouring to make was why we should proceed by this method to risk our ability to pay what we promised to pay with respect to the "A" class of shares, by doubling the capital and borrowing the money, and running the risk of leaving in the hands of the bank, not in the hands of the government, an investment of $10,000,000 upon which 4J per cent interest is to be paid. What we really have done by this bill is to provide for borrowing $5,100,000 of money, and banding it over to the bank to invest in such a way as we hope will bring us a net return of 4J per cent. That is the situation as far as I can see it. That may be the tactics of a schoolmaster, as the minister says, but I am endeavouring to be enlightened, and I would like to have some further information on that point. I never have been able since I saw the bill to understand why any government found it necessary to double the capital of the bank for the purpose of being able to name four directors with two votes each. The only thing that need be done is to expropriate the $5,000,000 of shares outstanding. That was even discussed in this chamber on one occasion; the now Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) made some references to that method when discussing the report that came from the banking committee.

With respect to the other point, the government believed that ownership normally in this country is represented by authority and control, and that it would be fairer to everybody concerned for the government to be an investor along with the other investors if it proposed to take control of the institution. That is to say, the government takes control of the institution not by force majeure but by an actual investment by the country in excess of the investment of private investors, thus justifying the government in assuming complete control of the institution by majority control and ownership.

This bill will give the
government greater control over the bank's policy, and therefore when we vote on this bill we will be voting on the question whether we are in favour of the government being given greater control. In view of that fact, could the minister tell us briefly what the policy of the government will be in the matter, whether it will differ materially from the present policy, and if so in what way?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
I think I attempted, Mr. Chairman, in the address I made on the resolution preceding the bill to outline the factors which enter into considerations such as those now expressed by my hon. friend. I can tell him quite frankly that in justice to the great interests of the people which must be served in this matter I should be doing them a disservice if to-day I indicated to this House of Commons what the present policy of the bank is with respect to its day to day transactions. I should be doing those great interests a disservice if I indicated what

the policy of the government would be in connection with the major policies of the bank. If, for instance, just as an illustration, I indicated that it was the policy of the government, and therefore the policy of the bank, steadily to expand the volume of currency and credit, such statement by me from this place would be taken by everyone as an invitation to speculate in commodities and stocks because there would be the maximum possible assurance of a rising price level, depending upon the extent to which that policy was followed. There must be from day to day, from week to week and from month to month, by the experts in the employ of the bank, by the executive board of the bank, and particularly by the governor and deputy governor, and communicated to the Minister of Finance from time to time in order that he may be informed, continuous study of all the factors that have to do with the economics of this country in so far as they can be affected by monetary policy. I am not one of those who believe that monetary policy is the only factor in the economic welfare of the people. Many tend to exaggerate its importance, but at the same time I do not want to minimize its importance. When we have, as we have in Canada to-day, a managed currency, managed by the Bank of Canada, which obviously becomes a definite instrument of government policy, that materially increases the responsibility with regard to a declaration of policy. 1 can say in broad terms that I should regard a policy of deflation as utterly out of the question under the conditions which prevail to-day, but as to the extent to which any policy opposed to deflation may be applied, it must be a question of continuous study of all the factors entering into the problem on the part of those who are trained to assess their value and their effect, along with other factors, upon the economic life of the nation. I do not think I should be asked to go further -than that in this matter.

If anyone should tell me that the right of ownership to a share of stock in a joint stock company was such as the minister has suggested, then he would have to overrule several decisions of the courts of this country. Minorities have rights in joint stock companies, and no majority holder of shares, whoever he may be, even the crown itself, can exercise his rights in such a way as to impair the rights of the minority. The decisions of the courts are clear on that point, so long as they act within the sphere of their rights. All that was necessary was to expropriate fifty-one per cent, or, as I suggest, sixty per cent of the $5,000,000 of shares, representing $3,000,000, and a single section would have given the government the right to acquire by expropriation or negotiation, at a, price that might be agreed upon, the sixty per cent of shares in the concern. And having acquired them they would then have the power to elect the four of the directors. But, as brutally put by the minister, the ownership of an interest in a joint stock company being of the type that he has indicated, I think there is some question about it. But once more, that may be merely the schoolmaster's view and not that of one who has knowledge of the subject.

I have not been able however, nor am I yet able, notwithstanding the explanation given, to understand why the doubling of the shares of this bank was done in that way, when we know that $5,000,000 is not necessary for any purpose of the bank; and the minister has declared the reason why it was done.
What I have never been able to understand, since the minister made his statement when he introduced the bill, is why the acquisition of sixty per cent of the shares of the bank would not have served the purpose. To assert the holders of shares in the bank had a misconception or a misunderstanding of their position is entirely beside the question. They all knew that they had made an investment that would give a four and a half per cent return, and they knew that the bank was under the control of the government, indirectly and not directly. What is changed is the method or form by which that control is being effected; and to increase these shares by borrowing an additional $5,100,000 to put in the hands of the bank to endeavour to secure the whole $10,000,000 at four and a half per cent, when money can be borrowed at as low as less than one per cent-that is, short term money, treasury bills-is something that I have never been able to understand. The minister's statement is that this is the policy of the government, and that has always been a complete answer, to say that it is what the government wishes to do.

speechtext:
Section 20, which is
being repealed, reads:
(1)	Whenever the capital stock of the bank has been subscribed and payment in money made to the amount of twelve dollars and fifty cents per share, or such larger amount as the minister determines, the minister, when authorized by the governor in council, may issue a certificate authorizing the bank to commence business on a date to be fixed therein.
(2)	The bank shall not issue notes or otherwise engage in business until the date fixed in such certificate except to do what is necessary or advisable to enable it to commence business on the said date.
What we did was to take a number of the officials and make them provisional directors, and they carried out all the antecedent prerequisites of a corporate organization to enable the bank to function; and this section is one of the conditions prerequisite to its functioning. Now it is being taken out of the statute so that when you refer to the consolidation of the Bank of Canada Act you will find this section gone and no section providing in any way for what is in that section provided for. It is always customary to leave in a statute everything that has to do with the organization of an institution. If anyone other than I were saying this, it would be regarded almost as an axiom that you would never do such a thing. However, I am not endeavouring to lecture the minister with respect to it; if I were to use the harsh

word that is in my mind with respect to it, it would but do justice to the occasion. It is almost absurd to think that this section should be taken out-absurd, that is, to any practising lawyer.

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
I have been waiting
patiently until we should come to section 13, which is, if I may use the expression, the operative clause of the act. I have not been very much concerned about the change in the set-up of t'he bank, for the very simple reason that the directorate, whether it consists of seven or fifteen or any other number, amounts to very little because no action of the directors can override the decision and the will of the governor or, in his absence, the deputy governor; and that is virtually the situation. I mention that because I was not much concerned about this discussion as to the change in the set-up of the bank. I do not think very much change has been made, except in form. What does concern me was contained in a question asked a few moments ago by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), regarding the matter of policy. The minister replied that in his opinion it would be inimical to the best interests of the bank and the country for him to enlarge in a statement on what the policy of the government or of the newly government-controlled organization, the Bank of Canada, would be.
I asked the minister when we were on the resolution-I think, in ample time-if on the second reading of the bill he would be prepared to make a statement with respect to that matter. No statement was made on the second reading, and no discussion at all occurred. Now, while I respect the delicacy of the situation, and, perhaps, the difficulty the minister finds himself in, I submit to him and to the committee that if we are sincere in what we are doing to give effect to what was said regarding this matter in the speech from the throne, and if we are to have confidence in the declarations of members of the government, including the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, who have spoken on this matter, we must recognize that the government is taking new and definite control of this bank. That is the only excuse for the presence of the bill. I still question the adequacy, shall I say, of the method, but that has been adopted by a majority of the house, and I bow to the will of the majority. If therefore the government is stepping into this picture in a new way, exercising what it claims to be adequate authority, and, as the speech from the throne says, taking effective control of the bank, I submit the committee is certainly entitled to a larger measure of confidence from the government as to its intentions in the future. In his reply to the hon. member for Acadia the minister used an adjective with which I agree; he said he would not make any statement regarding the "day to day" operations of the bank. It
would be ridiculous to suggest that the minister or any officer of the bank or other person should make a public statement as to the detailed or day to day routine operations of the bank. Now on the question of broad policy-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: What phase of it?

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
That is the object of my remarks, though perhaps it will take a few paragraphs to state it; as to the broad policy of the bank I think the committee is entitled to a greater measure of confidence from the government.
In order that I may not be considered presumptuous in making the suggestion I shall read a few extracts from the speech of the governor at the first annual meeting, on February 25, 1936, of the shareholders of the Bank of Canada. I pause to make the statement that the country and the bank are fortunate in having as governor and deputy governor of the bank two gentlemen who without question are clothed with ability and experience quite adequate for the positions they hold, and it is my opinion that during the time the bank has been in operation, within the limits of their powers, and, I might add, the policy behind the bank's operations, these gentlemen have discharged their duties in a manner commendable to themselves and commensurate with the task they undertook. Further, the bank has been in operation only a little more than a year, so that I am not expecting to see any very startling results up to the present. I think the experience we have had indicates that the central bank in its initial stages has been reasonably satisfactory, but I also believe, as the government, too, must have in mind, that we have now come to a stage in the development of the central bank where a larger measure of public interest in the institution should obtain. It is upon that assumption that I proceed with my remarks, and quote from the address of the governor. I hope the minister will note the language, in view of the fact that we are requesting him to give us some information as to the government's attitude and. policy. The governor says:
A policy of cheap and abundant money is the orthodox contribution of a banking system toward recovery from a depression. '
That is a very singular statement. We are still in a depression. Unemployment is still rampant throughout the country. We are still confronted with many problems

fundamental problems, in my opinion-regarding the causes of the depression, and I submit we have not yet directed sufficient attention to the removal of those fundamental causes. So that when the governor of the Bank of Canada makes a

Bank of Canada

statement of that kind, parliament at least should take more than ordinary notice of it. I repeat it:
A policy of cheap and abundant money is the orthodox contribution of a banking system towards recovery from a depression. Such a policy undoubtedly contributes, firstly, to a relaxation of the pressure to liquidate and, secondly, to a recovery of business and to the reestablishment of government finances, which are sure to be adversely affected at such times through relief expenditures and other unavoidable commitments; but if the policy is pursued too far the situation may become unmanageable when a revival develops.
Without indulging for the moment in any speculation as to what should be done or to what extent the government should use the resources and services of the bank in a contribution towards recovery from the depression, I cite this paragraph as indicative of what must have been in the mind of the governor of the bank, and it is more or less a challenge at this time for a statement by the government of the country, which is now assuming control of the bank, as to what is its attitude. I know of no place, Mr. Chairman, where this should be stated other than in this house; this is the place.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
I thought I said it a
few minutes ago.

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
While I recognize that
the minister feels he is in a delicate position, that delicate position cannot excuse him from taking the house into his confidence to the fullest extent possible, if necessary even to the point of having a private session of the house, which has been done under conditions not more serious than those obtaining in Canada at the present time. Since I have been a member of the house we have had on at least two occasions, I think, secret sessions. I am not suggesting that this should be done; I am prepared to have any discussion of this kind wide open, but I do say the minister cannot shield himself behind the statement that if he were to make any declaration on the subject it might prejudice the interests of the bank or of the country.
That is one statement I wish to direct to his attention. Then on the next page the governor makes a further statement, referring to advisory functions. I pause at this point to suggest that apparently the governor considered his duties largely advisory, but it must be remembered that this assumption was based upon the act as it was originally passed and the bank as it was originally organized. According to the speech from the throne and the declarations of the Prime Minister, however, we are making a change in that situation, and the government now

is to control the bank. In other words all the statements made by members of the government during the election campaign and in their criticisms of the original act two years ago, as well as the inference contained in the speech from the throne, indicate that they were not satisfied with the organization as it was originally introduced. Therefore I am justified in assuming that while the governor may have taken the position that his chief function was an advisory one in his relation to the government, if we are to be logical something must be added to this advisory function now. In that respect the governor has this to say:
Nevertheless, we have every inducement to be impartial. Advice must often, perhaps usually, be the chief form of assistance which we can render to the governments of Canada, inasmuch as our necessary concern for the cash basis does not permit us to make large advances of a kind which we cannot offset if that policy were requisite. It should not be inferred, however, that we are unable to furnish temporary accommodation at appropriate times.
The suggestion that occurs to me, from the language I have just quoted, is that under the old organization the governor of the bank considered that it was his duty to be extremely careful as to the extent he might go in regard to advances to the government or, as he says, in furnishing temporary accommodation; that he must be restricted because under the old set-up he conceived his duty to be largely of an advisory character.
Now I turn to another more practical and to my mind very much more vital part of the address, which I think is peculiarly appropriate to this particular section. Before I read it I will invite the committee to observe that section 13 amends the original provision that gave the bank power to do certain things, or in other words very largely defined the functions of the bank. I am not going into a detailed analysis of those functions; I merely invite the committee to consider the facts as they are outlined in that section. It will serve my purpose to cite just a few of these clauses. Paragraph (d) indicates that the bank may buy and sell securities issued or guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada, and now an amendment has been introduced changing the former limitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: Expanding it.

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
... buy and sell or rediscount bills of exchange and promissory notes endorsed by a chartered bank drawn or issued in connection with the production or marketing of goods, wares and merchandise as defined in The Bank Act, excepting those mentioned in paragraph (h) of this subsection, and having a maturity not exceeding ninety days, excluding days of grace, from the date of acquisition by the bank.
Before that paragraph passes I think the committee should consider whether sufficient latitude is permitted to the Bank of Canada in the powers of rediscount therein granted. Again I say it is a question of opinion, but I invite the minister and the committee to give consideration to that feature, because this is one of the powers which will enable the bank to enhance greatly the powers of the chartered banks in the discount market.
I wish now to read what the governor of the bank had to say on the subject to which that subparagraph relates. I quote from his speech of February 25. The heading is "Treasury Bill Market."
It is universally recognized that a central bank is hampered in its operations where an active bill market does not exist. Few countries, however, have the bill market they would like. Under present conditions a fairly satisfactory market can be established, if there is a sufficient volume of treasury bills, if there is a good institutional distribution of these, *md, in particular, if it is the commercial banks policy to hold treasury bills as their secondary reserve. The mere existence of a central bank at once widens and strengthens the market for first class bills, since the central bank itself will be a large holder and will 9nSage in purchases and sales in pursuance of its open market policy, and for other reasons. In so doing, it is likely to have the effect of
Bank of Canada

steadying the rate. The Bank of Canada can, I feel, claim that it has been of assistance in both these respects.
Canada has been handicapped, as the governor points out, by the absence of a fairly extensive bill market. We have not and cannot expect to have a bill market such as they have in London or New York, but the government can greatly assist if its policy is gradually to extend the bill market in Canada. The government could very well declare, without in the slightest degree impairing the present banking situation, or without any danger of encouraging wild speculation, as the minister puts it, that its policy will be not only to encourage the establishment of a bill market but to do everything in its power in cooperation with the Bank of Canada to secure the use of all the facilities that can exist in Canada for the encouragement of the buying and selling of bills. I shall not go into an analysis of the practice elsewhere, but I assume it is known to all that, for instance, in London a bill of sixty days or three or four months may pass through a dozen different hands during the period of its currency. I have seen bills that were endorsed so often that they had to stick on additional paper on which to write the endorsements. That is an active bill market; and a very small margin of profit, running to three or four decimals, is sufficient for the purposes of such a market. Nothing of the kind exists in Canada, but I can readily see how there could be built up in Canada an active bill market not only for government bills but also for commercial bills such as those indicated here. That leads me to suggest that possibly it might have been better if in this section the term of maturity had been made four months instead of ninety days.

speechtext:
I am glad the minister mentioned that, because I intended to refer to it. These, however, are what are known as active commercial bills dealt with in section (g) to which I have referred. The reason there was an enlargement of time in respect to the class of bills to which the minister refers

was this: Take for instance live stock. It was found it was not possible to merchandise live stock within ninety days. Frequently those who were handling live stock on credit through the banks found that they were forced to liquidate prior to the time that the stock was fit to sell. Your market might on a certain day or certain week or weeks be so low that it would be unprofitable to market. And so it was found that so far as live stock and some other products of that class were concerned a larger period should obtain. However I am speaking .of rediscount, bills of exchange, promissory notes and the like. They are more along the line of what might be called ordinary commercial paper. I suggest therefore that the minister would be quite within his rights and would not in any way jeopardize the interests of the bank or of the. country if he made clear to the house what is to be the attitude of the government in regard to these and indeed other matters which in my opinion are vital to the operation of the Bank of Canada and its relation to the government and the problems of the country.
Another point I might very properly raise has reference to the production of gold. In this connection I shall give the figures for the last seven years. The production of fine ounces of gold for each year during the period 1929 to 1935 was as follows:

Canada is one of the largest producers of gold; I believe it is now in second place, although in the last year or two Russia has challenged our position in that respect. However it is safe to say that in the production of gold we are one of the first three countries. The question which occurs to me is this: What is to be the government's policy as to its control of the Bank of Canada in regard to the holding of a larger quantity of gold? In the disposal of gold what form or general policy will be adopted? If we are simply to take gold and use it as a commodity, exporting it as it is produced to the markets in New York and London, and occasionally in Paris, are we exhausting our possibilities under a system of finance operating through the Bank of Canada? The question might be asked: Has the government considered the advisability of retaining in Canada a larger portion of gold produced?-because I find

that the export of gold in the seven year period I have indicated almost equals the total production. Although I have not the figures under my hand, may I say that by checking I found that the export of gold practically equalled the production. Is it advisable to consider increasing Canada's reserve of gold and under existing laws making use of that reserve? I am quite aware that there is a distinct cleavage of opinion, but I do submit to the minister that with respect to these matters to which I have referred, and perhaps other matters to which I have not had time to refer, he might reasonably give the house a statement of government policy. While, I repeat, I respect the minister's sense of delicacy in dealing with these matters, surely if the government of Canada is to acquire and exercise control over the Bank of Canada, parliament has a right to know at least the broad general lines of policy of that bank operating through the new control, namely the government of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not in mind quite the class of question the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) has raised. I do not think the hon. member who asked the question about the broad policy to be adopted had in mind the matters to which the hon. member for Kootenay East has referred. I did not make note of his various questions as he proceeded to speak, because I expected each one would be the last, and up to a certain point I had succeeded in keeping his remarks in my mind. If in replying I do not cover all the points, perhaps the hon. member will come to my assistance. I had prepared some observations which I intended to use in reply to questions addressed to me a few days ago by the hon. member, and perhaps at this time it might be well to give expression to them.
The process of affecting our price level by monetary action is not nearly as simple as some would have us believe. Under certain conditions the price level will rise even if there is some decrease in the amount of cash in the country. Under other circumstances the price level will fall even though the cash is increased. Because of the introduction of greater weight, for the time being, of some other factors, conditions change from day to day. So that a policy in regard to cash which is proper in May may not be proper in June, even if the goal towards which we wish to move remains the same.
I believe it would be incorrect and improper for me to indicate my personal opinions or to appear to voice the opinion of the government with regard to the objective which we should attempt to attain in the matter of the price
level, or to indicate by what monetary policy I thought that objective should be attained. Such an indication would give individuals an opportunity to anticipate any action which might be taken, and to reap a profit and in fact would be a far more serious indiscretion than advance information on the budget. May I invite the attention of the hon. member who asked the question to the fact that by creating uncertainty and apprehension we might interfere with or at least impede the realization of any desired objective. As a matter of fact, to a certain extent that has occurred in the United States, due to announcements in advance of objectives. Immediately upon an announcement being made, forces were started in motion which tended to impede the very desirable objective it was sought to attain. I think however it is quite in order for me to say that any suggestion that a deflationary policy is being pursued is incorrect, and any suggestion that a deflationary policy should be pursued is contrary to common sense. The views in regard to price levels which have been embodied in the declaration of more than one conference, so far as I am aware are still held in this and other leading countries of the world. My hon. friend may recall that in speaking on the resolution preceding the bill I made certain statements as to the functions and duties of the bank. In so far as those words indicate a policy, I shall repeat them. At *that time I stated that when a boom is under way and getting out of hand it is the duty of the bank to put on the brakes by restricting credit, thus tending to cause a decline of prices, and to slow down the whole tempo of business and speculative activity. Conversely, in a time of depression, it is the duty of the bank to bring influences to bear in order to extend credit, thus tending to raise prices and quicken the tempo of business activity. The only criticism I make of my own words is that they might be taken to indicate that I share the views of those who believe that monetary policy is all important as an influence upon the economic life of a country and its people. I stated earlier this afternoon that I do not believe that. It is one of the major factors, it is true. Its importance changes from time to time, having regard to the weight for the moment of Other factors. There are periods when it is all important; there are other periods when it is of no importance at all, temporarily at all events.

A few moments ago I tried to show how the revealing in advance of an objective to be attained, through the management of currency, remember, lets loose forces which defeat the objective sought. Now, why is that? The answer is very simple. Immediately the objective is announced, if it be an objective of a higher price level, let us say, what happens? speechtext:
There are three or four questions that I should like to direct attention to with respect to this particular clause. The clause, as it is proposed to amend it, indicates perhaps more clearly than any other the desirability of a new institution having an opportunity to demonstrate its usefulness before drastic amendments are made either in its powers or in the exercise of its ordinary functions. This bank has been in existence for a short time, and during that period it has given an excellent account of itself. It has had time to issue only one annual statement which has been published, and that statement has been referred to during the progress of the discussion this afternoon. Among other functions which the government imposed upon the bank was that of acquiring the silver which had been purchased under the provisions of the silver convention. The loss to which the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor) referred could not under any circumstances be a loss if the silver were utilized for coining purposes, for the profit upon coining would be more than equal to any loss that could occur by reason of the difference between the price at which the silver was bought and the price to which it had fallen; that difference is substantially less than the profit accruing to the government from the coinage of silver, as indicated the other day by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer). But, as regards the question of the note issue of the bank, it will be observed that by section 13 it is now proposed to expand the powers of the bank by providing that it may-
(d) buy and sell securities issued or guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada or any province having a maturity exceeding two years from the date of acquisition by the bank, but the bank shall at no time hold such securities
having a par value in excess of fifty per cent of its outstanding note issue and deposit liabilities.
Its note issue at the date of the last annual statement, that is December 31, 1935, was roughly $100,000,000, plus its deposit liabilities, which on that particular date happened to be about $200,000,000, and the half of the two would make altogether, roughly $150,000,000. That is, the bank shall at no time hold such securities having a par value in excess of $150,000,000 on the 31st day of December, 1935-
... nor shall the bank at any time hold such securities maturing more than ten years from the date of acquisition of a par value in excess of three times the amount of the paid-up capital and rest fund of the bank.
The rest fund is $173,000-one can eliminate that for the present-and three times the present paid-up capital would be, roughly speaking, $30,000,000. I suggest to the committee that that departure from the provisions of the statute, to which great consideration was given, is one which might bring about great disaster to the bank if the powers were exercised, and I am one of those who hold that it is not desirable to clothe a new institution with powers unless we expect them to be used. As the statute stood before this amendment was suggested, it contained all the powers that, in my judgment, could reasonably be conferred upon the bank, having regard to later conditions which obtain or are likely to obtain in this country during any period of time that we can anticipate. The provision, therefore, with respect to investments should have some more adequate explanation than we have had so far. I do not know why it is thought desirable by the government to change that condition, to have the acquisition of securities of a certain type, namely those of the provinces and of the dominion, based upon some relation to the outstanding note issue and deposit liabilities, for I frankly fail to see the relation between the two, and to say that the bank shall at no time hold such securities which have a par value in excess of, as I have said, practically speaking, in terms of the last annual statement and of the new capital, $150,000,000. On December 31 last the bank held dominion securities amounting in all to $114,000,000; fifty per cent of its note issue at that time was $50,000,000, and fifty per cent of its deposit liabilities at that time would be another $100,000,000, making altogether a total of $150,000,000. But at that time the dominion banks had on deposit $18,000,000, and the chartered banks had their reserves deposited with the bank to the extent of $181,000,000,
Bank oj Canada

That is the position as shown by the statement, and I should like the minister to explain why it has been thought desirable, after but one annual statement has been issued by the institution, to modify in the manner indicated the provisions of this paragraph (d) of section 13.
There is another point, which has been alluded to by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens)-he mentioned it the other day but he did not develop it-and which I had proposed to speak about at some length. I am clearly of opinion that this bank should acquire a greater holding of gold, and if I were asked the reason why, I would, as a schoolmaster, refer to the explanation given by the minister himself on the page opposite page 6 of the bill as printed:
This enlargement of the bank's power to hold securities with a maturity exceeding two years is necessary, partly because of the deletion of the words "exclusive of securities transferred to the bank under paragraph (c) of subsection three of section twenty-five," and partly because during the course of the next ten years the chartered banks will lose the right to issue approximately $100,000,000 of bank notes and the Bank of Canada's note issue will be expanded correspondingly. Other things being equal, the Bank of Canada must acquire an additional $100,000,000 in assets as an offset. In view of the scarcity of short term_ securities it would not be practicable to restrict the bank to the purchase of securities maturing within two years.
That calls for but two observations. One . is that the development in this country of a market for short term securities

the bill market, as it is familiarly known in England, or more particularly, in Lombard street-can come about only through this bank participating largely in the first instance in these operations. Second, the bank has power to issue four dollars in paper currency as against every dollar of gold that is held as coverage. Would it not occur to most people that, by acquiring another $50,00,000 or $75,000,000 of gold and paying for it with Canadian legal tenders, the bank would be enabled to take care of any situation which might develop, instead of having recourse to the provisions suggested in the accompanying note? If the bank is to function in the manner indicated, according to the powers which we have conferred upon it, not by this act but by another act, namely in the issuing of paper money-using the colloquial term one hears on the street-if it exercises those powers to the extent that in another statute we have provided, it must acquire the gold coverage to enable it to do so, and gold coverage acquired at $35 an ounce to the extent of an additional $75,000,000, or even $50,000,000. would confer upon the bank a power of issue that is limited only by the provisions of the statute.

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: The bank has that power now.

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: That is what I am speaking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: I mean, it has the gold now.

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
I am obliged to the hon. gentleman for his information, but I may inform him I am quite well aware of that fact. I thank him for his generous exposition of his own knowledge for the purpose of assisting me, but I am already aware of that fact. Being aware of that fact, I am merely pointing out that it may be advisable to add to the gold reserves of the bank for the purpose I have indicated, and in that event the bank would accomplish that purpose without much difficulty.
At the appropriate time, when this section was under consideration, I intended to say that I was wholly in accord with what was said as a mere suggestion the other day by the hon. member for Kootenay East. I had intended to elaborate upon it, but I shall not take time to do so now. I think, however, the acquisition of an additional $50,000,000 of gold at this time would serve a very useful purpose. It would keep in Canada that much bullion which would be available for the purposes provided by the act, and at the same time the purchase of that gold would release in this dominion that amount of money in Bank of Canada bills, what is colloquially called paper money. If the Bank of Canada acquired a thousand ounces of gold it would pay $35,000 in Bank of Canada paper money or bills which, as hon. members have said so frequently in the house constitute legal tender in this country. Inasmuch as the government has complete control over the matter and no gold can be sold outside Canada unless a licence is issued for its export, while I do not suggest that it is desirable to acquire a very large quantity of gold at this particular moment or that, I do suggest that we should be constantly accumulating gold, for what was said yesterday by the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Caban) is something which is not very frequently discussed.
The export from this country of $40,000,000 of our gold reserves by a former Minister of Finance had a most detrimental effect upon our whole financial structure. That, I think, is admitted by people who are students of the situation within or without Canada. So seriously did we regard the matter, Mr. Chairman, that at a caucus of the party with which I was then associated in opposition I asked members of my party not to make any reference to the matter at all, because I believed

Bank o] Canada
that it would not be in the interests of Canada that certain possibilities, which as a matter of fact later became actualities, should be developed. It was found that certain people outside the country took action, which I think it was well understood would be taken by certain astute gentlemen, and it was because we had incurred a risk, which risk had been realized by others, that we suggested that in the public interest nothing further should be said about the matter. Nevertheless, because of that action we were 840,000,000 of gold coin short in this country, and when I say "short" I mean that $40,000,000 of gold was utilized for the purpose of discharging a New York liability, which action lessened to that extent the amount of gold reserve held in this country. That could never be made up; as a matter of fact, in the early succeeding days after England went off the gold standard there was a diminution in our supply of gold coin and bullion until we could take the necessary action under the relief act to regulate the export of gold and provide that it should not be shipped out of Canada except under licence. For it must not be forgotten that Canadian banks, with head offices in Canada, are doing business in many countries. In the very nature of things the branches near at hand may 'depend upon the free movement of gold from the head office to meet any situation that may suddenly arise. When that right of free movement is changed it becomes necessary to consider every transaction in the light of meeting the difficulties that may arise in the country in which the bank may have the particular branch.
We had to deal with that question when we provided for the revaluation of gold coin at the time we took over the gold from the banks, and we provided that a certain portion of that gold should be treated as gold which was held for foreign reserves, using the word "foreign" as meaning all reserves or liabilities external to Canada. Under those circumstances I have thought, perhaps improperly, that we should add to our store of gold for the purpose not only of meeting the situation that must arise during the next few years in connection with the retirement of the paper money issued by the bank, but also of replenishing our stock of gold to something beyond the amount we held after there had been a diminution in our stock through the shipment of $40,000,000 of gold to New York. It is true that the revaluation of gold has increased the amount that appears after the dollar sign in the annual report of the bank. It is true also that we conferred upon the bank certain stabilizing powers with the profit which accrued through the revaluation from $20.67 to the current market rate on gold prevailing at the
time the changes were made. The act itself was never proclaimed, but in the annual report of the bank "other assets" appear at the very substantial sum of over $3,250,000 and "liabilities not otherwise disclosed" amount to something over $2,000,000. So I assume that there has been a utilization, to some extent, of the profit that does not appear in the balance sheet except under the two items I have mentioned. Of that, of course, I have no knowledge except such as might be derived from the reading of an ordinary balance sheet.
Those three points, therefore, I suggest should be considered: First, the question of silver, to which reference has been made, and which I think takes care of itself; second, the question as to investments, which I think, calls for some wider explanation than we have received. In the drafting of that section originally great care was exercised lest we should provide a credit condition which would be injurious to the bank itself, and the restrictions imposed were of a double character. First, we had regard to the fact that the bank now holds a substantial quantity of Canadian securities as assurance against its guarantee or liability when it took over the Dominion of Canada notes. The exact figure I do not carry in my mind, but it amounts to several millions of dollars of Canadian securities held by the Bank of Canada for the purpose of indemnifying it against any liability which may attach by reason of it having assumed the obligations of the Dominion of Canada in connection with what we used to call the old dominion legal tender, or the note issue of the dominion itself. That expansion of power I find it a little difficult to understand; certainly the enlargement of the power for the reasons given is hardly sound finance, because it involves the acquisition of securities for the purpose of taking care of this additional note issue when the effective and profitable way would be to acquire gold when it carries with it a right of issue such as that mentioned in the other statute to which I have referred. And with respect to the acquisition of gold, without developing the subject at greater length, I think by reference to leading authorities I oould give good reasons why we should gradually increase our holding. I shall not say more, because I do not desire to trespass too greatly upon the time of the committee in this regard.

In the very nature of things this central bank must discharge an ever-increasing respon11'-bility, if there is an improvement in commercial conditions, for the simple and obvious reason that the chartered banks cannot provide money for their customers and at the same time have it locked up in long term securities. No. I wonder why this disputatious matter should have been thrown into the cauldron of politics at this particular time. Nothing has given me more concern than to find this provision in the bill at this time, having regard to the very difficult conditions under which we live. I do not propose to refer to the political side of the matter, and at this time I speak only for myself. It is not a matter which I regard as in any sense affecting those associated with me as a party. I have said quite freely that they may take any view they consider desirable. But speaking as a Canadian with as tolerant a point of view as any man in this chamber, and yielding to no man in my tolerance and my regard for the views and attitude of mind of every other Canadian, I find it difficult to understand why this question is now being precipitated into the debates of this chamber.
A short time ago we made a trial of what I thought was a not unreasonable suggestion, namely that all persons in Canada of French origin who so desired could obtain bills of the Bank of Canada printed or engraved in the French language. That in itself was a concession. It was admitted by everyone that it was a concession. My view is that very great changes, from the purely constitutional view, have been brought about by the tolerance, good will and kindly thought and appreciation of Canadians of one class who were content to accommodate themselves to the views of others. But when we enact in a statute that every bank bill in Canada shall be engraved in two languages we have created a situation which will involve in every session of parliament an effort being made to repeal.

That will happen as regularly as the sessions come; I am speaking as a result of experience. I must accept a large measure of responsibility for the provision of the law as it now stands. That provision stated that notes in either the English or the French language shall be available as required. I can point out only that the most strenuous supporters of the rights of our fellow French-Canadian citizens, as expressed by, for instance, the late Senator Belcourt, both in writing and in oral argument, rest upon the assumption that where an ethical group occupied a position in a country such as Canada before confederation or, in fact, before it became a part of the British empire, there was a common law right that they should speak their own tongue and be able to understand the business they had to transact written in their own language. The contention thus made is one which has found substantial agreement in the tolerant minds of their Anglo-Saxon fellow citizens, or those of other descent.
Let us look at the situation. The constitution deals with it in one way. But if I were in the province of Quebec to-day, before dissolution of the legislature, and I were to receive the orders of the day, I would not receive that document or the journals printed in the two languages side by side; I would have to take my choice. I would have freedom of choice. My fellow-member of French descent receives his orders of the day printed in French; my fellow-member speaking the English language and of British descent receives his in the English language.
In this parliament what is the position with respect to the statutes and journals? I am discussing a bill. I walk to the table and take from it a bill printed in either English or French. But the bill is not printed in columns, one English and the other French.
I take my choice, exercise my freedom of action. I have conceded, because the statute so provides, the right of my fellow-citizen who clings, as Senator Belcourt pointed out in one of his addresses, to his own language. He selects from that table his French copy; I, my English. The orders of the day, which we have before us for this day, are printed in both languages. My French fellow-member has in his hands Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day, but he is using a document which is printed in French. I happen at the moment to be using one printed in English. I exercise my right; he exercises his. He chooses the one printed in French; I choose the one printed in English. The statutes are in exactly the same position.
But we have gone further. In a spirit of tolerance and mutual good will, when we cele-

I may say that even that concession brought about much criticism, and I should like to point out to this committee that the criticism went so far that in some cases we received letters with a mutilated bill, protesting, in language that I shall not repeat, against this action being taken. My answer in all instances such as that was this, that we had during a long series of years, in a spirit of the utmost good will and from a desire to conciliate differences and promote harmony, provided that a choice should be exercised by our fellow-Canadians of French origin and those of other origins, and that they might have bills, paper currency, printed in the language they desired, as their fellow-Canadians speaking other tongues might have bills printed in English. That freedom of choice was greatly resented in some quarters, and strong protests with respect to it were made to me personally from time to time. Now, Mr. Chairman, we are to be told that this gesture is to go to the extent of having all
paper money issued by the Bank of Canada printed in English and French; that each language shall appear upon the bill. Is that quite fair?

When we did deal with the Bank of Canada we extended the principle of choice. That is, I repeat again, my fellow-Canadian citizens speaking the French tongue and of French descent would have in their possession bills, paper money, which was printed or engraved in the French language, and equally, English-speaking citizens of British descent could have in their hands and in their pockets bills engraved or printed in the English language.
Let us go a step further. The majority have the rights which are provided by statute; the minority have the rights which are provided by statute, from a purely constitutional and legal standpoint. From a purely legal and constitutional standpoint we deal with only a limited number of matters. Now I put this to my friends who have pressed this so strongly: In the light of the development of a spirit of amity and good will, a tolerance and a desire for harmony, many concessions have been made. subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: So far as legal tender is concerned, we have provided that, if required, the money from the issuing power shall be printed in either English or French. The courts have said repeatedly that this is a country in which there are two official languages. The late Senator Belcourt pointed that out in one of his arguments, and I do not think there is any answer to it. There are two official languages in Canada, but this is not a 'bilingual country.

The difference is so
obvious that I know my hon. friend does not require an answer. There is a limitation with respect to the one and not to the other. The official language is provided for by section 133 of the British North America Act. That deals with constitutional rights, and the right creates the official language. But when you come to the question of official bilingual-

ism you find that it does not exist. In this country, I repeat, we have two languages. I am not unmindful of the fact that during the last ten years there has been great agitation in some parts of Canada in connection with this matter, and it has been urged that it should be dealt with as is now proposed. I am not unmindful of the fact that it has been made the football of politicians, and that is the reason I am refraining from making any political observations regarding this matter. I do not propose to do so however great may be the provocation. I point out, however, to my fellow countrymen who are of French origin and speak the French language that those who will take the evidence of history for what it may be worth-and it is fairly important-will find that wherever the granting of a privilege or a concession by a majority has by the minority been crystallized into a right, resulting in a pushing of the demand beyond those moderate and reasonable boundaries that have marked the maintenance of harmonious relations between majorities and minorities, the consequence has been harmful to the minority. I plead, uselessly I admit, with the government not to do this thing at this time. We have at the moment great differences in this country, differences which we all deplore, differences the outcome of which we are fearful of, differences which threaten the very fabric of our confederation. Why not give a fair trial to what now is on the statute books? It has been there only a year; why not give it a trial? Why not let the demand for a change come about by that gradual process which would ensure that those who are most affected, namely, the majority, who are of British descent and speak the English language, will feel, as they do not now feel, the desire to do something further in a spirit of amity and good will? Why not do that? Why force this at the present time upon the people of this country? Why force it through parliament with the government's majority? Why do that? I cannot understand it, because this step that was taken in the Bank of Canada Act was a step further in advance, so far as my fellow Canadians of French origin are concerned, than any step which has been taken since confederation. It gave them the opportunity which, as I have pointed out, is the basis of all arguments that have been made to secure their bills, currency, from the bank printed in French as well as in English.
Now, to say that the will of the minority shall prevail over the will of the majority of the people of Canada is to create as dangerous a condition as it is possible to

Bank of Canada
create. I am not a prophet, but I venture to suggest that this provision will create such a situation that every session will see a demand for its repeal. Just as regularly as the session comes someone will rise in his place and move for leave to introduce a bill to repeal it. I say that in the light of the experience which came to the former government between the date of the passing of this statute and the time we left office. I say it seriously to my fellow Canadians. It has nothing at all to do with my relations to party. I have told my friends, as I repeat, friends having business with me in matters connected with the party, that my view has nothing to do with the party view or with the view they hold. I am giving, however, my own experience from the time we placed this provision on the statute books until the moment we left office, and I know whereof I speak. I say, in the best of good feeling and most seriously to my hon. friends: Do not do this thing. Do not do it now. I say that in view of communications which came to me personally, some abusive, some insulting, none commendatory. They indicated a condition in this dominion which I did not think existed. But if it brought about a resentment so great, criticism as harsh as that to which I have referred, because we provided for a free choice of language, either French or English, what will the situation be when we compel the majority to accept the decision that ultimately all the paper money of this country shall appear in the two languages? That is the issue. Never in my time have I been so much moved in my desire to prevent what I know will result from this action, and I am not guessing about it. It is a conviction in my heart of what is inevitable, from communications I have received, and from statements made to me. I know we are doing something that we shall deeply regret. I wish to say a word or two about this particular section, inasmuch as I mentioned the matter in connection with the second reading of the bill. The history of the world, in my opinion, has been the history of minorities, but the history of Canada has been the history of compromises. Majorities seem to have no rights and can 12739-231
get nowhere in this country. The principle of compromise was effected by confederation, section 133, on the bilingual question, and was distinctly set out in the British North America Act, and there has been no change in this respect in any of the decennial revisions of the bank acts that we have had from 1867 down to the introduction of this section 15. The law distinctly sets out what are the rights of minorities to the French language; they are governed by the British North America Act. Confederation was a compromise. I have a great admiration for the qualities of the French nation, for all they did in the great war. The untold privations and human sufferings, the trials and tribulations, the anguish and suffering they endured for the good of humanity will stand in the future among the brightest pages of the most sublime patriotism in the history of the world. As I say, confederation was a compromise on this question. What was that compromise? It will be found in section 133 of the British North America Act, and the end of it was to be there without any extension, as follows:
133. Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
The acts of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
My views on the second reading of this bill will be found in Hansard of June 2.
We had no banking legislation in this country, from 1867 on, other than in accordance with the provision for the revision of the bank acts every ten years which was silent on that point. Section 60 of the Bank Act on note circulation is more or less overridden by this new provision contained in section 15 of the present bill. For all these years we have been getting along very well together, and I might' point out that there was no objection when the banks, for their own purposes, and purely as a banking measure in certain communities which were largely French, made a certain issue of bilingual notes according to the population and the business done at those branches. Had I been here I would have opposed that concession then. But now it is proposed to write that into the law of Canada and make legal all notes in French of the Bank of Canada. There is only one way to go about this thing if it is to be done legally. I contend that section 15 of this bill is a violation of the letter and spirit of confederation as set

Bank of Canada

out in section 133 of the British North America Act. Indeed there is no doubt about it. Section 133 lays down the law. Section 15 of this bill, I contend, is unconstitutional, and I am opposed to any extension of the principle it involves and of any compromise already made, but I believe the proper way for those who support this measure to go about the matter is to apply for an amendment of section 133 of the British North America Act, and then by way of the Bank of Canada Act, and I am opposed to any such amendment. I might point out that since the law was passed we have had the following innovations: one, federal blue book issued in two languages; two, our postal stamps were changed bilingually; three, bilingualism has secured a foothold even in the Ontario public school system, and a concession or compromise was permitted to allow a few notes in French for the use of branches in Quebec, in practice. And now parliament, by section 15 of this bill, is asked to issue notes in the French and English language. You cannot compromise on a great public principle. No doubt one side of a ten dollar note of this bank will be French and the other side will be English.
My stand on this matter is that I am absolutely opposed to any extension of the British North America Act along these lines. I have not an ounce of bigotry. I speak in this parliament sincerely and honestly what I conscientiously believe to be the truth and the whole, truth, and I never change my views! I support principles, and they are fixed and admit of no compromise.
In conclusion, I contend that this section is against the spirit and letter of the British North America Act and the purposes of the fathers of confederation; everything that was done by them along these lines we are now going to undo. The matter came up in 1934 in connection with a French bill, before the banking and commerce committee, and this parliament laid down that section 133 was the law. The various finance ministers since confederation at every decennial revision of the bank acts were opposed to any change in the direction of introducing a bilingual note, until section 15 of the Bank of Canada bill was here introduced. The Liberal party headed by Mr. Fielding was opposed to a bilingual bank note, and various finance ministers on both sides since confederation took the same stand; they were absolutely against the principle of this bilingual section. It is going to lead to untold confusion in connection with the circulation of these notes, some of them internationally. Further, there is no demand for such legislation. The matter was not discussed in the last election. I never heard it mentioned anywhere in
[Mr. Church.)
Ontario. I know the views of the people of Ontario. This note circulation clause of the Bank of Canada bill is copied from section 60 of the consolidated act of 1934 regarding banks and banking; the principle of that section is copied into the Bank of Canada bill with the bilingual feature added. I am not speaking for all the people of Ontario, but I believe I speak for some of the people of Ontario who are opposed to any bilingual extension of the British North America Act along the lines indicated, especially when it is recalled that Mr. Fielding, a former Liberal finance minister, and the banldng and commerce committee a few years ago took a very strong stand against any innovations or changes to make bilingual notes legal tender. The Prime Minister last Thursday night laid down a rule for minorities which he expressed in the following words:
The principle I am laying down is that there is no minority which is superior to the majority when that majority is the people of the country as a whole; and the people of the country as a whole have sent this present House of Commons to legislate.
They did not send this House of Commons to legislate to change the British North America Act and to have bilingual notes foisted on the people over their heads, and to upset the views held by all the finance ministers since confederation. I wish to protest against this dangerous change. It was never discussed in the constituency I represent. I have always argued sincerely and honestly along these lines; I shall continue to do so, and I believe I am taking the right stand in strongly opposing this innovation that is getting into our banking system, in the way I referred to it on the second reading of the bill on Tuesday, June 2. We have the Macmillan report; it is silent on this bilingual question. The various commissions took it for granted that this matter had been settled at confederation forever. I would have opposed any recent concession had I been here, and if necessary alone. I refer to the Royal Commission on Banking and Currency; I see there no reference whatever to bilingualism in their report. I have read the report three times; I studied the findings and the dissenting judgments given by one or more of the commissioners, and examined the index, and I could find no reference to or suggestion of any demand for bilingual notes in Canada. Why not leave things alone? As matters stand, those who need bilingual notes can get them at the French branches by applying to the branch office of the various chartered banks. I have consulted four or five bankers and they all tell me that there is no necessity for this bill; it is more of a political bill for

Bank of Canada
political purposes than it is a banking or economic bill. For that reason I am strongly opposed to it, and I believe the people of Ontario and the English-speaking majority are strongly opposed to it and to any extension under confederation of section 133 of the British North America Act, which was a contract made with the people of the old provinces of Canada. To any extension of that principle I am strongly opposed, and I will vote and speak against it at every stage of this bill, because it is against the letter and spirit of confederation.

Mr. Chairman, before proceeding with the few remarks I intend to make, I wish to congratulate and thank my hon. friend from Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) for the kind words he has just uttered. He spoke as a true Canadian! I hope and trust that the views he has expressed- will grow and spread throughout the Dominion of Canada.
(Text) I shall try to make my few remarks in answer to the speech of my right hon. friend this afternoon as moderate as I can, and I must congratulate the right hon. gentleman on the moderation of the language he used in discussing this matter. I shall even say that I believe my right hon. friend to be sincere, but he is desperately and dangerously wrong in the sentiments he has expressed. My right hon. friend is sorry that this matter is being, as he said, precipitated into the political field. Will he pardon me if I say that he is the man who is precipitating this matter into the political field? I shall even say that I am sorry my right hon. friend said that he expects this matter will come up at every session in the future, and that there will be motions for repeal, and so on. These words, coming from him, are almost a threat; at the least they are an invitation to do the very thing which he deplores.
I do not believe this will happen. If you look at the matter, Mr. Chairman, I think it is very simple. Before this Bank of Canada Act was introduced by my right hon. friend there were banks in Canada issuing their bills in both languages. The Banque Canadienne Nationale has branches not only in the province of Quebec but all over Canada; the Banque Provinciate du Canada has branches not only in the province of Quebec but throughout Canada, and the notes of those two banks are and always have been bilingual. I have in my pocket a five dollar bill of that type, but I shall not show it in these dangerous times. The parliament of Canada has taken away from these various banking institutions the right to issue notes. Under
Bank of Canada

the act as it stands this is to be done gradually, but in a few years there will be in this country no other bank notes in Canada than those of the Bank of Canada. I ask every fair-minded man in this committee whether it is right that the French population of this dominion, who have always had their bank notes printed in their own language, should be deprived of that right by the parliament of Canada.
