speechtext:
I am
coming to that, and probably that is the very reason why my right hon. friend and his government did what they did. That was not a concession, as my right hon. friend has said so many times. I come back to that word "concession," which I do not like. We are not conceded the right to live or to breathe the air of this country. We have that right. It was not a concession. There always have been bilingual bank notes in Canada, as my good friend from St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. White) said the other day in his fine Canadian language. He showed that even before confederation there were these bilingual bank notes, and my good friend, who is as broad-minded as they make them, said that he was in favour of the change proposed by this bill. But mind you, Mr. Chairman, there was something else to justify making it compulsory that there be notes in both languages. Under section 133 of the British North America Act both languages are official in this parliament in the federal courts and in the courts of the province of Quebec. These bank notes are legal tender. As such they will be deposited in the federal courts and in the courts of Quebec where both languages have a right to exist. Surely it is right that these bank notes should be in both languages. I said in 1934, when I proposed the very amendment which is now embodied in this bill, that I was congratulating my right hon. friend on recognizing and acknowledging that this was to be done. What I was criticizing at the time, and what I criticize to-day in his attitude, is the method by which it was done. The moment you concede the thing should be done I cannot understand why there should be two opinions about the right method.
My right hon. friend speaks of the rights of the majority. First, let me tell him he is wrong in assuming to himself the right of speaking for the majority. In this house a majority of the English-speaking population of Canada is represented on your right, Mr. Chairman, and there is also a majority of the French-speaking population represented

on your right. In what way could the rights of the majority be infringed by this amendment? I tell my hon. friends on this side of the house or on the other side, when anybody in Canada, whether during an election campaign or otherwise, blames them for the stand they are going to take in this matter, to ask those who criticize them if they prefer to have a bank note all in French if they are English-speaking, or all in English if they are French-speaking, or to have their own language on one side and the other language on the other side. After all, the bank notes issued under my right hon. friend's legislation are legal tender everywhere in Canada. You can pay a $10 debt in Ontario or Saskatchewan with a $10 bank note in French; no one can refuse it. But would not any man be better pleased to have a note with his own language that he can read on one side of it, if he cannot read the other side? I repeat that I cannot find any ground for the objections which are being set forth against this proposal. They are absurd.
In other countries there are some wise people too. I challenge anyone in this committee or elsewhere to show me a bank note of a country in which the language conditions are as they are in Canada, which bank note is not bilingual or even trilingual. Take Belgium; the bank notes there are printed in French and Flemish; in Switzerland there are three languages on the bank notes, French, German and Italian, and it is not so bad after all. In our commonwealth of nations there is South Africa where they have the same condition as in Canada, the bank notes are in Dutch and English. In the Irish Free State they have the two languages of the country on the bank notes. In no country of the world have they two sets of notes, one set in one language and the other set in the other language. Why should we have this stupid thing in this fine Canada of ours? I cannot believe tnat there are people in my country who are so narrow as not to see that it is better to have a bilingual bank note than to have two issues, one in English and one in French.
My right hon. friend says that under our constitution there must be two different sorts of documents. It has always been so, he said; you have the documents of the house in French and English, giving you the right of selection. If you prefer them in French you take the French, or if you prefer the English you take the English. This is so as a matter Of convenience, because the document is less bulky, and for considerations of that kind. But is it so because of the constitution? I have imder my hand the rules of this parliament as issued from time to time since

Bank oj Canada
confederation. The first book of rules was issued in 1868, and in it one sees exactly what nay right hon. friend said is not done in Canada. From the beginning they had one page in French and the alternate page in English, throughout the book. I have the books of 1876, showing exactly the same thing, and in 1896 the same thing. Since then it has been thought more advisable to have one book all in French and another all in English. But this was done not because of the law of the land, not because of any constitutional provision, but merely as a matter of convenience. I have before me similar books from the Irish Free State.
Let me say also how awkward it is for the banks to have to keep two sets of bank notes in their various branches where they have customers who ask for French notes or for English notes. To do so complicates the business of the banks for no good reason whatsoever.
Now, let me refer to what my hon. friend said, and dwelt upon for quite some time, that Canada has two official languages but is not bilingual. My hon. friend the member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) asked him a question which he disregarded but which was very proper. May I read to my right hon. friend the words of a man who has left his mark on the history of Canada, a man who was the leader of the party which is now led by my right hon. friend. Let me read to my right hon. friend the words of the greatest Conservative leader of all time in Canada, Sir John A. Macdonald, and I shall ask my right hon. friend to compare the words of that great leader with those the right hon. gentleman uttered this afternoon. Those words are found in the debates of the House of Commons for 1890, column 745:
I have no accord with the desire expressed in some quarters that by any mode whatever there should be an attempt made to oppress the one language or to render it inferior to the other; I believe that would be impossible if it were tried, and it would be foolish and wicked if it were possible. The statement that has been made so often that this is a conquered country is a propos de rien. Whether it was conquered or ceded, we have a constitution now under which all British subjects are in a position of absolute equality, having equal rights of every kind-of language, of religion, of property and of person. There is no paramount race in this country; there is no conquered race in this country; we are all British subjects, and those who are not English are none the less British subjects on that account.
I commend those words to every Canadian, in this year 1936. They are as true to-day as they were at that time. I note with pride that my hon. friends opposite are laying
wreaths at the base of the monument to Sir John A. Macdonald in Kingston. All I wish is that his ideas may grow and germinate in this Canada of ours, and that all - those who claim that they are his disciples; that they learned their political views and ideas from what he taught them in days gone by, may adhere to the views he then expressed, and stand by the principles which he said should prevail in all the Canadian provinces.
I believe I might be permitted to relate an incident in my life. Some years ago I had the honour to represent Canada on the assembly of the League of Nations in Geneva. At that time a question of minorities which had been annexed to other countries after the treaty of Versailles was being discussed and debated. One gentleman, a prominent delegate in the assembly and at that time president of the confederation of Switzerland, Monsieur Motta, said this to the delegates of the world there assembled:
In Switzerland we have no minority problem. We are three races living here side by side. I belong to the race which is less populous, namely the Italian race. One of the two other languages I do not speak. I have been elected twice as president of this republic, even by men whose language I do not know. We have no minority question; we are all equal. No person in Switzerland believes that there is one controlling or dominating race or language, and I cannot see why those problems are discussed in other countries constituted as is Switzerland.
I wish that in Canada there may be no minority problem and that we should all act towards, live with and treat- others as Canadians, purely and simply.
I will tell my right hon. friend that at this time in my own province I have read speeches made by young people who advocate the separation of Quebec from confederation, and the creation of a new French country. They claim that they cannot have their rights recognized in -the Canadian federation. They are wrong; I have told everybody that they are wrong. From my seat in this house to-night I tell them that they are wrong. Even if their plans were carried out they could not achieve what we have achieved in confederation in building up a great free country. The same advice I give to those who think that people of my race should form a party of their own, and should not join one or the other of the great parties which divide public opinion in Canada. They, too, are wrong. Let us adhere to that party the prevailing ideas and principles of which are nearer to those held by us. It is desirable that no political party should be based on racial lines. The view which is sometimes expressed reminds me of the Roman Emperor
Bank of Canada

Caligula who used to say that he wished that all the Romans would have only one head so that he might cut them off with one stroke. I do. not think that is desirable for any minority or any part of a country.
We should continue as we are. We should plead with our friends, our brethren from the other provinces in Canada, to join hands and hearts for the greater development of our country. My right hon. friend has pleaded with me; I plead with him when I say that I do not think it is wrong on the part of those people who speak my language to want to have bank notes with words in their language appearing thereon. I do not think that is wrong. Surely I cannot be branded as a narrow-minded nationalist. When I came to this house I could not speak a word of English; that was many years ago. Had I shared the views of some of my fellow-citizens in Canada I would not have undertaken the drudgery of acquiring that little knowledge I have of a language which at that time was so strange to me. It meant work to acquire that language. I thought I was acting as a good Canadian when I undertook to study it. Surely my hon. friends from my native province who are sitting here to-night are in the same position. It cannot be asked that they be considered only as people who are having concessions handed to them, as my right hon. friend has said. I plead with him not to use that word "concessions" any more either here, or anywhere else in Canada. We do not want any concessions. We do not need any concessions. We do not ask even privileges, we ask simply the right to live as we have lived. There are nine generations of my family buried in this country. I do not need concessions in Canada or anywhere else, and I believe no man or woman in Canada will accuse us of asking too much when we ask what is embodied in this amendment to the Bank of Canada Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after listening to the wonderful speech delivered by our good friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), I hesitate to speak. On the other hand, as an English-speaking Canadian I should like to express my opinion on this subject because I took a stand upon it in the banking and commerce committee when the former government introduced its legislation dealing with the Bank of Canada.
I do not think that in this Canada of ours we should be going backwards, nor do I think any member of this house or any of the people of this country wish that. I have in my hand a piece of money coined in 1837.

On one side is engraved "Province du Bas Canada-deux sous," and on the other side "Bank token-one penny," and the coin carries the coat of arms of the city of Montreal back in 1837.
I have another one before me, and on one side of it are the words "Province du Bas Canada-deux sous"; and on the other side "Bank token-one penny." This coin also carries the coat of arms of the city of Montreal, and is dated 1837.
I have before me another one, and on one side appear the words "Province du Bas Canada-un sou," and on the other side "Bank token-halfpenny, 1837." This also carries the coat of arms of the city of Montreal.
Another coin I hold in my hand has on one side the words "Lower Canada," in English, and on the other side in French "Un sou, 1837, Agriculture Bas Canada."
I have before me another coin, and on one side appear the words in English, "Quebec bank token, halfpenny," and on the other side in French, "Province du Canada, 1 sou, 1852," and bearing the coat of arms of the city of Quebec.
Another coin I have in my hand has on one side the words in French, "Province du Canada, deux sous"; and on the other side in English, "Quebec bank token, 1 penny, 1852."
When you go into other countries you find that in Belgium, for instance, the coinage is printed in French and in Flemish; in Japan you find an entirely different situation from Canada as to nationalities; yet the Japanese currency is printed in both the English and the Japanese languages. I find the two languages on this Japanese coin, one yen, and its English equivalent.
In China there are many languages, and their coins nearly all carry the English language as well as the Chinese.
In German West Africa, where we find German, Arabic and Dutch people, we find two languages printed on their coins.
On the coinage of British North Borneo we find the English and Bornese languages used.
In East India the coins are printed in both English and Hindustani. In India itself, where they have four principal languages, and in several other countries we find about the same principle carried out in the coinage.
But here we are to-night in the parliament of Canada making almost an issue of the use of the French and English languages on the paper currency of Canada, and after what I have said, Mr. Chairman, of the practice in other countries I am, to say. the least, very much surprised at the discussion that has taken place on this clause. I considered my French-Canadian fellow-citizens as heirs and

Bank oj Canada
joint heirs with me in the development of this country of ours. I consider them neither my inferiors nor my superiors, and all I ask is that we go forward hand in hand together to develop and make this Canada of ours what we all wish it to be. Some people may think this is a very small matter, some may think it is a large matter; but I would say that nothing is too small to create animosities and hard feelings which may prove a very serious hindrance in the development of this country.
May I give to my English-speaking fellow-members an outstanding example of how the two great races in this country can get along together in amity? In the city of Sherbrooke, in the county of Sherbrooke, back in 1881, the first French-Canadian mayor was elected for the city. At that time the population of the city of Sherbrooke was very largely Englishspeaking Canadians, about eighty per cent English to twenty per cent French-Canadian. In the municipal council there was one French-Canadian and all the rest were English-Cana-dians; yet with a couneil so overwhelmingly English a French-Canadian mayor was elected for the city. What has been the result of that act- of equality and of generosity, not of any concession, which was the term used by the leader of the opposition? The result was that two years later an English mayor was elected, and when his term had expired a French-Canadian mayor was again elected. To-day the city of Sherbrooke is eighty per cent French-Canadian and twenty per cent English-Canadian, but that same tradition has been carried down through all the years, an Englishspeaking mayor for two years and then a French-Canadian mayor for two years. I quote that example because it shows the sense of justice and fair play that has animated the two great races in this country in the city of Sherbrooke since 1881, and I hope the practice which has prevailed ever since will always continue.
I shall not delay the committee further beyond giving one more example along the same line. Only two years ago a French-Canadian mayor of the city of Sherbrooke who had filled his two-year term of office, in view of the change in populations, decided that he would seek a second term. A great discussion took place, and finally an English-speaking citizen ran against the French-Canadian mayor whose term of office had expired, and to the honour of the citizens of Sherbrooke, when the ballots were counted in every single French polling division in the city a majority was given to the English-speaking mayor, showing the great sense of justice and fair play that animates our people. That is the reason why I am so keen that we do not call this "concessions." Our French-speaking fellow-citizens do not want concessions, and so in conclusion I would say: Let us play the game fairly and squarely; let us join hands one with the other whether French or English-speaking; let us have bilingual currency in this country of ours and show that we want to play the game fairly regardless of race, religion or nationality.

speechtext:
This is not a matter on which I wish to speak at any length, Mr. Chairman, but in case there is a vote I wish to place my own personal position before the committee.
Two years ago when the legislation setting up the Bank of Canada was before the house the bill was reported from the committee and at the last moment there was introduced an amendment, as I recall it, along the lines of the clause now before us. I voted against that amendment, not so much on the merits of the case, I must confess, but because I resented an amendment of that kind being introduced at the last moment when it could not be adequately discussed and because it was dealing with a matter that was so likely to arouse a good deal of discussion and perhaps bitterness.
I must say that as between the two plans, the one of having a bilingual currency and the other of having two sets of notes, as at present, my judgment is that the bilingual currency is preferable, and for that reason I personally shall have to support the legislation as it is before us to-night, even though I voted against an amendment along this line previously introduced. And yet, in saying that, I regret that the government has seen fit to make the change at this time. I listened to and was very greatly impressed, as we all were, by the eloquent speech of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). But I do not think that in matters of this kind the question can be settled simply as one of right or wrong; it is much more complicated than that. The English-speaking people of Ontario, or at least a great many of them, start from one set of premises; the Frenchspeaking people and even the English who reside in Quebec start from an altogether different set of premises, and there is no point at which these two sets of arguments meet. After all, the problem resolves itself largely into a conflict of fundamental ideas which people hold to most tenaciously. I think there was something in what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) said, though I regret his use of the word "concessions," that unless we are very careful in Canada we may easily introduce matters which will prove very inflammable indeed, and for my part I would say that our French-Canadian friends will have to exercise just a little bit of care
Bank of Canada

not to be too aggressive in pushing their particular point of view, just as I feel very strongly that the English speaking-population have sometimes been prejudiced with regard to these matters of language and so on. For my part it is a matter of indifference whether we have bills printed in both languages or not; it is not important at all from my standpoint. I say, however, that if we are going to carry out the spirit for which the Minister of Justice pleads we shall 'have to recognize a little more clearly than we do the point of view of others in Canada and not to press too aggressively our own viewpoint. I know that is a little vague and it is an ideal which it is very difficult to attain, but I felt that to-night I ought to give my own point of view. That some of my colleagues may not think as I do merely emphasizes the fact that such questions provoke personal reactions and that a good deal depends upon how we weight this or that factor in the problem.
Mr. DUNNING; Naturally, a number of considerations were in the mind of the government in dealing with this matter and in drafting this particular section. I take the view that the question of principle, in so far as there is a principle, was adopted in the year 1934 by the parliament which preceded this one, but the principle was applied in a manner calculated, as experience has proved, to produce rather than to allay the kind of friction to which reference has been made. There is a marked difference between printing separately in each language the routine proceedings of this house-which any one of us may accept or reject-and printing separately in each language legal tender which passes from hand to hand. We have plenty of evidence of the objection to the present method. Frequently protests come to me, as my right hon. friend admitted they came to him, from English-speaking parts of Canada. Why? Because French bills had turned up there. There is no means whereby the turning up of English bills in Quebec or of French bills in other parts of Canada can be prevented, and there is complaint on that score. I say that a more intelligent method of dealing with the matter is to put both languages on the same bill. The parliament and the government of Canada during the course of many years have recognized the desirability of this method in matters of currency. For example, I have in my hand a Canadian postal note, the kind of postal note that has circulated in Canada these many years, printed in both languages on its face. I have before me a Canadian postal money order circulated in these terms in Canada these many years, printed in both languages.

I have personal reason to know that prejudice can be aroused by these documents. I am one of those who have suffered politically because of my belief in this matter. In 1930 the candidate supporting my right hon. friend made the most, and in the most public manner, of what is called the French language issue and promised without qualification that if his party were returned to power French on these postal notes and post office orders would be removed. This did not happen. But I say that if we were right in 1934 in providing for French separately in connection with currency we ought consistently at the same time to have provided for separate English and French postal notes and postal money orders.
Now, with regard to the purely practical aspect, may I point out that the method at present in use is expensive to the bank. It involves two separate sets of plates for every note. If that can be reduced to one, there is a saving of $29,000 in connection with any new note. The existence of the two different sets of notes involves, of course, separate sorting of the stock and the turn-over. Think of it-and the turn-over. Although the demand for French notes is experienced chiefly in Quebec and Ontario, it is necessary to keep a stock of both at all the agencies of the Bank of Canada right across the country, because we are required to make the notes available in either language throughout the dominion. The need to sort the notes as they are paid in nearly doubles the labour of sorting in the important agency of Montreal and considerably increases it in Ottawa and Toronto. This is indeed the chief extra cost which is incurred.	Both	English	and French bankstend to pay into the central bank notes which do not suit their requirements as to language, and it therefore follows that the total receipts and reissues of notes are greatly increased above what would normally be the case if the notes were bilingual. Before that section is carried there are some matters I should like to speak about, and it is my intention to move an amendment to section 26 of the act. It will be remembered that last year and again this year I introduced into the house a bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act in respect of the remonetization or greater use of silver. On both those occasions this bill was thrown out by the Speaker as not being in order, but on both occasions only fifty per cent of the proposed measure was criticized by the
Bank of Canada

Speaker. The particular matter I have in mind this evening is in connection with subsection 4 of section 26, which is the clause relating to the agreement signed by Canada in London, in 1933. The present clause in the bill reads thus:
(4) The bank shall during the years 1935, 1936 and 1937 purchase and hold newly-mined Canadian silver as and when required so to do by the minister, but the bank shall never be required to purchase more than 1,671,802 fine ounces in any year.
In my opinion this should not have been placed in the Bank of Canada Act at all. This was in accordance with an agreement signed in London in 1933, when, I believe, some twenty-six countries attended. At that gathering a resolution introduced by the United States for the greater use and the adoption of silver was finally disposed of by certain nations agreeing to do certain things within the next few years. The United States, Canada, Australia, Mexico and Peru agreed to purchase between them 35,000.000 ounces of silver during the years 1935, 1936 and 1937, and other countries, including India and Spain, agreed not to sell over a certain amount of silver during those same years. This was introduced into the house, and, as I said, should have been in a special bill and not have been placed in the Bank of Canada Act. Of the 35,000,000 ounces, the United States agreed to purchase 24,421,410 ounces; Canada agreed, as I have pointed out, to purchase 1,671,802 ounces, and the other countries I have mentioned agreed to purchase the balance. Briefly, that is the history of the London conference agreement, but I want to draw particular attention to one word in the Bank of Canada Act which I do not believe exists in any other statute of this country, and that is the word "never." It says in the Bank of Canada Act that the bank shall "never" during those years purchase more than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: It does not say "never."

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
The act says that the bank shall "never" during the years mentioned be required to purchase more than 1,671,802 ounces. When the matter was before the house I endeavoured to have that word "never" taken out. I asked for an explanation, and I think it is pertinent to the amendment I am offering to read the remarks of the then Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) as they appear at page 4262 of Hansard for June 25, 1934:
The word "never" is probably an undesirable word to use in a statute, but it was put in this bill for a definite purpose, namely to prevent false hopes being created in the hearts of those who might be concerned. During the currency of the world's agreement it will be observed by the hon. gentleman that every-
TMr. Reid.]
thing depends upon the agreement being kept. And India, being tha key to the situation and having agreed as she did agree, we have added these words to indicate what our position will be. because we will have more silver than we will know just what to do with.
Right there, Mr. Chairman, the right hon. gentleman was in error in stating that we would have more silver than we would know what to do with. In the mint at that time they had between three and four million ounces of silver which was being used for the issuing of coins, but at that time none had been purchased under the agreement. During the past few days we have heard a great deal about living in the days of ox carts, but I wonder how many members realize that in spite of the up to dateness of our so-called monetary system in connection with the issuing of cheques and credit, the faith of the people of the world still clings to the precious metals. When I mentioned that of silver I want to point out that sixty per cent of the population of the entire world still use silver in their everyday transactions and still look upon it as real wealth.
I realize, in advocating this change, that most people fear that the printing press will be turned on, but in the short time I am going to take up I am going to try to show that we have here something that will act as a kind of a brake and a stabilizer, if I can use that word, against the issuing of unlimited paper money. Confidence is the one thing the people must have in their currency if we are to cany on without panic or disaster, and we must also have discernible limitations. I am going to endeavour to show that silver is one of those discernible limitations, and I maintain that we should add it to gold in connection with the further issue of paper currency.
The present valuation of our gold, which is roughly $180,000,000, has been brought about by the action of the United States, which raised the price from $20.67 per ounce to, roughly $35 per ounce. In this country we are getting the benefit of that action. No one can say how long that arbitrary value will remain; it may drop or rise again to-morrow. I listened with a great deal of attention to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) when he spoke of uncontrolled inflation and mentioned what happened in Germany. I should like to point out to the hon. gentleman that the value of the United States dollar in the markets of the world has not been reduced by the issuance of millions of paper silver certificates. It is true that when gold was revalued at $35 an ounce the dollar dropped to about sixty cents, but after the issuance of silver certificates by the United States the value remains

Bank of Canada
at about the same figure. The policy of the United States is worth noting. They have undertaken by statute to purchase silver until the silver reserve amounts to twenty-five per cent of the gold held by that country, and they are paying for the silver without going to the banks and borrowing money on which interest must be paid. It must be borne in mind that the silver certificates, one of which I hold in my hand, are just as valuable as the Canadian dollar, if not more valuable. On its face the silver certificate says, "one dollar in silver payable to the bearer on demand;'' while if one looks at our bills one finds that all one can do is to exchange one piece of paper for another. So, if it comes to having something tangible, the United States dollar may have the edge on ours, and in a case of a panic it might be in greater demand because it is backed by a precious metal.
What has Canada done in regard to silver? I should like to point out, first, that Canada is the third largest producer of silver in the world, with the United States the leading nation. In 1935 Canada produced 10,000,000 ounces of silver, so this country has a great deal to gain by recognizing this metal. We are trying to extend our trade with the United States, but in my opinion we slapped the United States in the face when we inserted the word "never" in this act, saying that we were not going to raise false hopes in the hearts of people with regard to silver. It may be that no leadership is going to come out of Europe and that by turning to the orient and South America the United States is going to take the lead in the Pacific as far as trading is concerned. If so her silver policy will play an important part. To carry out her policy she will still have to buy well over a billion ounces of silver, and I may say that at the moment she is buying practically all the newly-mined silver produced in Canada. Last year I believe the United States made a profit of some $19,000,000 on the newly-mined Canadian silver. When the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, (Mr. McGeer) was -speaking the other evening he endeavoured to outline the profit that was accruing to this country in regard to silver and the silver dollar. He was not quite correct, nor was the Minister of Finance correct when he stated that we were making no such profit. My information comes from the master of the mint, and it may interest many hon. members to learn that on every silver dollar issued we make a profit of between sixty and seventy cents.

speechtext: Net or gross?

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Gross. As has been pointed out, in Canada silver coins are eight-tenths fine, and there are three-fifths of an ounce in each dollar. Each ounce contains 480 grains. If the silver in our dollar were pure each dollar would contain 360 grains, but it is only -800 fine. Until 1921 our silver coins were -925 fine, but in 1921 the act was changed and we reduced the percentage of silver in our coins until now they are -800 fine. So a silver dollar actually contains only 288 grains or six-tenths of an ounce of silver. If silver is bought on the world market at forty cents an ounce, as it has been bought at times, the actual cost of the silver dollar is only twenty-four cents. But, irrespective of the price of silver, every ounce of silver minted makes $1.60 in coin, so that if an ounce of silver costs forty cents there is a gross profit of $1.20 on every ounce minted.
At one time this country produced as high as 30,000,000 ounces of silver a year. In 1910 there were produced 32,869 264 ounces, and it might interest the committee to know that there were at that time engaged in the industry approximately 15,000 men. Last year the production was not as great; we produced only some 16,000,000 ounces, and there were engaged in the industry only some 1.500 men. To-day we are looking for employment for our people, and right here is something which we can produce in abundance and which is in world demand. Here we have in our hills, especially in British Columbia, a product which is in demand in most countries of the world and will certainly be in demand in most countries of the world for some time to come by our neighbour to the south, which country has to buy well over a billion ounces if they fulfil their agreement or statutory requirements. Of course our bankers do not like that idea, as we would be making money or currency without any interest and naturally they would be against that. Those who trade in money are the ones who grow rich; the others grow poor, and the United States, by giving the lead in silver may well, as I say, become the leading trader in the orient and Pacific countries. We at least should have supported the United States in her silver buying policy.
Many countries to-day are turning to silver. One notices when a panic takes place, as has taken place in France, that the first thing
Bank oj Canada

the people do is to get hold of either gold or silver and hide it or take it out of the country. Some day there may be in the world a perfect system under which all business can be done with paper money, but until that time comes we have to do business with the world as other countries want us to do it. I repeat: There are over 1,200,000,000 people in the world who use silver or live in silver using countries. It may be said that we might disrupt the world if we went on a silver basis. I realize that if the economic affairs of a country are changed too quickly, this might lead to confusion, but I noticed the other day in this connection that experts are now claiming that if Great Britain paid her debt now to the United States this might create havoc in that country. It is questionable, of course, whether that debt will ever be paid. I am advocating, however, that greater consideration should be given to this silver question. The trade of the world, it should be noted, can be paid for in only two ways, either in goods or in some currency acceptable to the country which is selling the goods. It was when barriers were raised by each country against others, and countries were forced off gold, that the tragic circumstances of unemployment with its consequent distress which we have witnessed during the past few years took place. There is not enough gold in the world to finance the world's trade. Three countries practically control it all. I believe the United States is up against the financiers of the old world, who are endeavouring to cling to the gold fetish, but it may well be that the United States by her silver policy will compel those nations to come back to the old system and again use silver along with gold. In Canada we could well use all our silver. The leader of the opposition this afternoon talked about gold going out of this country, pointing out that it might be well to keep that gold here-

I am proposing an amendment to take out the word "never" and to make the amount mentioned in the London agreement, namely
1.671.802	fine ounces the minimum amount instead of the maximum amount as at present. I move in amendment:
That subsection 4 of section 26 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
(4) The bank shall purchase and hold newly-mined Canadian silver as and when required so to do by the minister, provided that during the years 1935, 1936 and 1937 the bank shall be required to purchase and hold not less than
1.671.802	fine ounces in any year.
Before the amendment is put I should like to say one word more. I know the statement will be made that the bank is not prohibited from purchasing silver, but if hon. members will read the act as it stands to-day I think they will agree that this is a prohibitory clause, and that the bank cannot purchase unless the minister says so. When we examine the present clause we find it states that the bank shall during the years 1935, 1936 and 1937, purchase and hold newly-mined Canadian silver as and when required so to do by the minister. Stopping at that point one would conclude that the minister could order the bank to purchase more silver. Then, if one reads the balance he will find that the act actually prohibits or precludes the minister from ordering the bank to purchase more, because it states that the bank "shall never be required" by the minister to purchase more than 1,671,802 fine ounces. My amendment does not interfere with the first paragraph; it permits the minister to purchase silver as and when he requires to do so, and it makes the London agreement amount the minimum rather than, as at present, the maximum. This will be at least a gesture towards our neighbour to the south who is endeavouring to cut a new path and to bring
about, if possible, stabilization of world currency, if I may use that expression. I would ask the minister's very favourable consideration of that which I have now placed before the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
The change involved in the amendment is that the minister's power to require the bank to purchase newly-mined silver is extended indefinitely. By the subsection now existing the minister's power extends to the years 1935, 1936 and 1937, the language of the statute being:
The bank shall during the years 1935, 1936 and 1937 purchase and hold newly-mined Canadian silver as and when required so to do by the minister ...
And for the time being I shall stop at that point. The amendment is that:
The bank shall purchase and hold newly-mined silver as and when required so to by the minister-
Without any limitation on the minister's power to require the bank so to do to the three years involved under the present law. Then, the proviso is changed, because the law as it stands at present is:
. .. the bank shall never be required to purchase more than 1,671,802 fine ounces in any year.
The amendment is:
. .. provided that during the years 1935, 1936 and 1937 the bank shall be required to purchase and hold not less than 1,671,802 fine ounces in any one year.
I am inclined to the view that on both these counts the amendment is out of order. The first suggestion enlarges the minister's power to require beyond the year 1937, and the change from "never be required to purchase and hold not less than" to "shall be required to purchase and hold not less than," is out of order as a measure which could be introduced only by a member of the government and with the approval of his excellency.
Mr, REID: Before the question is put, may I say that I am sorry the minister has taken that attitude. When I put my views before the house on a previous occasion this part of the proposed change was never touched upon. Exception was taken to the first part. It was pointed out that no member could introduce legislation involving an expenditure of money. I contend that it looks now very much like quibbling on words. I am endeavouring to give the minister power, but I am still permitting the Bank of Canada in the years 1935, 1936 and 1937, to purchase 1,671,802 fine ounces of silver. That is the real gist of the amendment. At the present time the bank cannot purchase one ounce more, and if hon. members will take the trouble to look

at the last statement of the Bank of Canada they will find that it has only two years' supply on hand. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while you are considering the point of order on the main question involved, may I call the hon. member's attention to the fact that the present act merely puts a limit upon the amount of silver which the minister may require the bank to purchase. It does not mean that the bank of its own volition could not acquire a larger amount of silver. Paragraph (a) of subsection 1 of section 21 of the act empowers the bank to buy and sell gold, silver, nickel and bronze coin and gold and silver bullion. The limitation in the section of the act now, under discussion is simply a limitation upon the minister's power to require the bank to do so and so. I point out that under another section of the act the bank has power to acquire silver. The limitation in this instance is upon the minister's power to require the bank to do so.
I cannot say anything further on the point, but possibly I might be permitted to give some general information on the silver situation as it applies to the Bank of Canada. It must be remembered that silver is a commodity subject to fluctuation, and indeed wide fluctuation in price. Last year the price of silver fluctuated from less than forty-five cents to about eighty cents per fine ounce.
Even the very small holdings of the Bank of Canada resulted in a loss of S489,368 to the bank between March 11 and December 31 of last year. The dominion government, of course, through the Royal Canadian Mint, and not the Bank of Canada, is the coinage authority of the country. The dominion government is at all times prepared to coin and make available to the public such supplies of silver coins as the public demand will absorb. Last year the silver dollar was issued for the first time, and so far 428,200 of these coins have been put into circulation. The 1936 silver dollar is now being coined; so far 205,200 of these coins have been put into circulation and the government has undertaken to coin as many silver dollars as the public will absorb. I should add that the Royal Canadian Mint has on hand a stock

of silver bullion amounting to approximately 3,000,000 fine ounces, which, based upon the average for the last ten years, is sufficient to take care of our normal coinage requirements for about ten years. That information I thought the committee should have with respect to the present coinage situation.

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
I wish to answer just
one point that was raised by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) who directed attention to the fact that I pointed out last year that we did not know what to do with silver on hand. As a matter of fact we had practically ten years' supply of silver on hand. That is what I meant to say, and we did not know what to do with it because, with the demand being as it was, we could not usefully coin it into dollars, quarters and dimes. That is the reason for the observation I then made. I had the same information on the subject as the Minister of Finance has given to the committee. I have thought-and I supported the thought by such action as we could take-of increasing the use of the silver dollar. There is in British Columbia an organization that has been urging very strongly the issuing in increasing numbers of the silver dollars. The special silver dollar that was issued last year met with a very considerable demand, but unfortunately not for currency purposes. Very few of these dollars were used, as a matter of fact, in the ordinary commercial channels, but they were put away as souvenirs. The coinage of a new dollar this year to the extent of $200,000 must add something to the circulation of silver dollars, but for some reason best known perhaps to those who are familiar with the psychological resentment against having heavy pieces of coin in one's pocket, the silver dollar except among the Chinese and others from the orient has not had a very wide circulation. As a matter of fact, I have never personally received in this country in recent years a silver dollar in change.
I think the hon. gentleman overlooked the fact that under what he was good enough to refer to as the London agreement there was a purchase of silver prior to the Bank of Canada Act coming into force, and the provision in the Bank of Canada Act that the bank should be the agent for the minister in acquiring the silver for those three years was introduced so that the bank authorities, those who had to deal with gold and silver bullion, should themselves make the purchases rather than the minister. I say that to the hon. gentleman because there was some silver that had been acquired by the Minister of Finance under the London agreement and that was

Bank of Canada
available for redemption purposes. That was what was meant by that provision of the section to which the hon. gentleman has referred. As to the larger question, of course, I have nothing to say.

speechtext: I should like to add just one word, and to ask the Minister of Finance two questions. I should like to know definitely if the bank is now empowered to buy or could buy all the silver it wanted.

speechtext: There is no question of that, as I understand the law.

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: If we are just going to put out silver dollars we shall never make any great headway. When I think of British Columbia and all its idle silver mines, which could put thousands of our people to work as they were at work in 1910, when 15,000 were employed in the silver mines; when I think that we could take over the product of those mines and pay for it without any cost to the country and strengthen the confidence of our people for they would know that behind the issuance of the silver certificates would be a precious metal which had an intrinsic market value apart from any monetary value placed upon it, and in view of the fact that the United States is going ahead and will purchase more than one billion ounces of newly-mined silver at the world market price, I think we could well consider what could be done in this country by taking our newly-mined silver at a guaranteed price and, as I said, without any cost to us at all. If we are looking forward to putting our people at work, this is one way in which we can do it, and it may be that the United States is giving a lead to the world. I believe she is bucking the gold bloc of financiers who are determined to keep the world on the gold basis. There are only three countries in the world to-day which have the gold to trade with, and the trade of the world has in consequence become stagnant- This is a question which the people can understand. It is as old as the hills, and as long as the people have faith in precious metals, as they have at the present time, we should look to our mines, take the silver we have and issue silver money or currency without cost to the government.

speechtext:
In view of what the hon. gentleman said in the earlier part of his observations respecting the attitude taken at the time the bill was introduced, I would point out that he has overlooked one fact, and that is that in 1910 India had not been put upon the gold standard, and silver then had a value in India, from the standpoint of
acquisition, which it does not now possess. The Indian situation is the one that complicates the whole question of silver. The accumulations of silver in India, as I pointed out in 1934, when the bill was in the form in which it was, are very large, and it was because India agreed to the terms of the London convention that it became effective at all. The hon. gentleman will remember that Senator Pittman is the great protagonist of the silver theory in the United States, and he was chairman of the committee that brought about the signature of the London agreement, but to do so he had to effect an arrangement with India, which arrangement was based upon certain restrictions that are indicated in the agreement which was tabled.
There is one other question apart altogether from the Indian situation, and that is that the policy resorted to by the United States has perhaps fallen down-perhaps that is not an unfair way to put it-because the price of silver, which was as high, I think, as eighty cents an ounce, certainly somewhere over seventy cents within the last fifteen months, has now dropped until it has reached the figure of, I think, twenty-two pence an ounce in London, and the price in America is the world price. That is the reason that in 1934 the provisions in the act were as they are. It will be recalled by the hon. member that the first function which the bank possesses is to buy and sell gold and silver bullion. That is one of its general powers. This was, so far as we are concerned, merely a matter of convenience when we put it into the statute to enable the Bank of Canada to discharge a duty which, under the agreement, rested upon the Minister of Finance.

I quote from Bourinot, 4th edition, page 407, chapter 13:
No eases can be found of any private member in the Canadian commons receiving the authority of the crown, through a minister, to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money. No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer. On one occasion, in the English commons the consent of the crown was given to certain formal resolutions proposed by a private member with reference to charges in courts of law to be defrayed out of the consolidated fund. It was thought, however, that any resolution placing a charge on the consolidated fund should be moved by a minister of the crown, and the more regular procedure was thereupon carried out. It was distinctly affirmed, however, that the member who proposed the motion involving the charge was within his right when he had the sanction

speechtext:
I can add very little to the explanation opposite the section in the bill. From the standpoint of administration the amendments are meant to make clear the intention of the original paragraph:
Under the old wording the "balances" held m the central banks mentioned might be balances in any currency. The new wording restricts the balances held as reserves to balances held in the form of pounds sterling, United States of America dollars and currencies which by law or in fact are convertible on demand into exportable gold.
The same change is made in regard to bills of exchange.

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
I really cannot understand how the author of the note can speak with such authority as to the intention in connection with this matter. It was quite the opposite so far as I am concerned. We were giving power to this bank to hold exchanges that were exchangeable in law and in fact for exportable gold. That was the whole point, and we did not restrict them to the limitations now imposed1. The section provided:
(b) foreign exchange, which shall mean-
(1) balances with the Bank of England, the Bank for International Settlements, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and a central bank m any country whose currency by law and m fact is convertible on demand at a fixed price into exportable gold.
That was done with malice aforethought, so to speak. It was intended that if it were desirable in the public interest to acquire either Belgian or Holland exchange, that might be done; especially was that true with respect to Holland exchange at that time. The effect of the amendment is that the definition of foreign exchanges is limited to balances in pounds sterling. I have some little difficulty about that, because some of the Scandinavian countries have so arranged their monetary system as, to use the colloquial language of the street, to tie themselves to the pound. It may be that the limitations
[The Chairman.]
at the end will remedy any difficulty in that regard, because it says:
-which by law and in fact are convertible on demand at a fixed price into exportable gold held in the Bank of England, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the Bank for International Settlements or a central bank in any country the currency of which is convertible as hereinbefore described.
What is the difference between the two? That is my difficulty: It turns the sentence around, but at the end of it it meets the difficulty to which I refer. When the hon. gentleman says that it was the intention of parliament to do so and so, I point out that the new section also provides for foreign exchange of the "central bank in any country the currency of which is convertible as hereinbefore described." It no longer applies to Belgium, but it certainly does to Holland, and that is what the original statute provided for, namely, any exchange that was convertible by law and in fact into exportable gold. There is, for instance, a limitation as to the minimum quantity that can be drawn. I believe that in some countries it is the equivalent of $4,000, and it is drawn in bullion and not in coin. But it is in law and in fact convertible into exportable gold. Reading the two sections, I should like to know, as a matter of information, just what the difference is.

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
This is an extraordinary section. It takes away from the shareholders the right to appoint the auditors and vests it in the governor in council, which, I think, is highly undesirable. Inasmuch as the Minister of Finance is made a shareholder for all purposes except one, and that one the election of directors, and that the ordinary right of shareholders still obtains with respect to class "A" shareholders, the appointment of the auditor should come from the shareholders and not from the governor in council. I can conceive of nothing that would be less calculated to inspire confidence than a set-up of that kind, by which the governor general in council is to name the auditors. That matter also was discussed considerably in committee. The auditors for, the present year have been appointed; it is provided that the governor in council shall make the appointment not later than January 31 in each year. This year the auditors have been appointed by the shareholders in accordance with the provisions of the law. I take it that this section would not be applicable until next year; then, when the shareholders meet, as they will, to deal with the report of the governor and the directors of the bank, they should be asked, I submit, to appoint the auditor, and the list or panel from which they shall make their

Bank oj Canada

choice is limited to the type of men who are auditors of chartered banks. Is it quite right to say that the governor in council shall name the auditors when you still continue to provide ownership with respect to class "A" shares, and class "B" shares, you have said, shall have all the rights and privileges which are incidental to ownership of shares except one, namely the right to vote for the election of directors? Should not the shareholders and not the governor in council elect the auditors?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: My right hon. friend is quite correct. There is no intention of changing the auditors selected last January, but it is thought that, having regard to the completely changed set-up and to the government control, the appointment of auditors should be the function of the governor general in council in such a case. It is a difference of view so far as my right hon. friend and I are concerned, but the government has considered the matter and desires to appoint the auditors of the bank, subject to the limitations contained in the section, which are that the auditor must be eligible to be appointed as the auditor of a chartered bank, and no person shall be eligible for appointment if he or any member of his firm has been auditor for two successive years during the three next preceding years. Provision is there for the changing of auditors in order that the audit shall not become stereotyped in character or get into a rut, but it is thought that the power to appoint should be vested in the governor general in council.

subsubtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Of course there is no function exercised by shareholders that has been more jealously guarded and more determinedly held than the right of shareholders to elect auditors. Directors have at times endeavoured to exercise that power, but the right of shareholders to determine who shall audit the accounts has been conceded, I think, in practically every case nowadays. It will be recalled that when Mr. McLeod of the Bank of Nova Scotia first set up the claim that there should be an independent audit of the banks, the banks objected to it and said that it was impossible to do it, but ultimately the right of the shareholders prevailed, and the banks are now subject to an independent audit. In the section we passed this afternoon we provided that shares issued to the minister shall carry with them the same rights and obligations as class "A" of the capital of the bank except that the holders shall not be entitled to vote at the election of directors. I am quite content to leave the section as it is, but never before in my time has the governor in council been 
clothed so frequently with the powers of parliament. If you take the statutes and read over, as I shall do presently, the number of cases in which this has been done, you will find that the governor in council is appearing more frequently than in any set of statutes we have passed in recent years. We are now taking away from the shareholders the right to elect their auditors and putting it into the hands of the governor in council, which cannot but be the very negation of modern practice with respect to banks.

This section is objectionable for a reason that has been frequently urged in this chamber. It gives the minister power to determine what are sheltered waters on the sea coasts of Canada. Such a power is not usually granted by any statute. It is a very important matter. Paragraph 55 of section 2 reads:
"Minor waters of Canada" means all inland waters of Canada other than lakes Ontario, Erie,	Huron	(including Georgian	bay),
Superior and Winnipeg, and includes all bays^ inlets and harbours of or on the said lakes and said Georgian bay.
It is now proposed to modify that by a new definition reading:
"Minor waters of Canada" means all inland waters of Canada other than lakes Ontario, Erie,	Huron	(including	Georgian	bay),
Superior and Winnipeg, and includes all bays, inlets, and harbours of or on the said lakes and said Georgian bay, and such sheltered waters on the sea coasts of Canada as the minister may specify.

Canada Shipping Act
That is, it clothes one man with authority to decide what are minor waters of Canada, on both Atlantic and Pacific sea coasts, regardless of any other consideration. I think that is an intolerable condition, if I may use language which sounds harsh. It is intolerable that in a country such as this one man may be clothed with that power, having regard to the purpose for which it is to be exercised. The purpose is abundantly clear in the explanatory note, which reads:
The object of this amendment is to give power to the minister to include under the expression "minor waters of Canada" as defined in the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, such waters on the coasts of Canada as he may consider comparable with the minor waters described in the said act. This will allow the masters of ships working in such waters to be men holding certificates for minor waters and in some cases temporary certificates. The only change in the paragraph is the addition of the words underlined.
The real crux is contained in this sentence:
This will allow the masters of ships working in such waters to be men holding certificates for minor waters and in some cases temporary certificates.
In other words, the minister has the authority to determine whether or not a given bay or inlet on the coast of British Columbia or on the Atlantic coast of Canada is a minor water. The same would apply to Hudson bay. Assuming that he decides a certain body of water is a minor water, as he alone may determine, he then has the right to accede to the request made that a man holding a certificate for minor waters, one who is not a navigator at all in the broad sense in which the term is used in the Shipping Act, or a man holding a temporary certificate, may take command of a ship that sails to and fro in those waters.
To a substantial degree that would cover *the coastal trade of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Quebec. As the paragraph now reads, without any limitation, it would cover the coastal trade on the Pacific coast. I protest against conferring such a power upon any man, however eminent he may be. So far as I know I have not seen any such power as is here contemplated conferred upon any minister. Just think what it means! One man is to determine that the inlets on the Pacific coast of British Columbia are minor waters. John Smith, a man with no certificate for deep water sailing, comes to the minister and says, "I have a minor water certificate. I am going to sail a ship and become master of a boat which has to do with trade in those waters." Or a man with a temporary certificate may approach a member or a supporter of the government, and that member or supporter
may say, ''Yes, I can fix you up," and in turn would say to the minister, "All you have to do is to declare that this is a minor water." The provision is supplemented that even with a temporary certificate one may operate a vessel in those waters, some of which are most dangerous. Nevertheless, that power is to be given. Had the former government attempted to do such a thing I believe I would have heard some hon. members now sitting in front of me speaking, from their then places in the house, about autocratic and dictatorial powers. This power does not cease to become that because it is exercised by a Liberal government; it is just as vicious in the one instance as in the other. To clothe one man with that authority is, I believe, a negation of the whole theory upon which the shipping act is based. After all, it deals with technical matters, with the lives as well as the problems of many people. When we clothe one man with authority to declare that a bay or an inlet on either the Atlantic or the Pacific coast is a minor water, and when in another section we confer upon him further power to clothe-putting it within the terms of the act-only reasonably qualified persons with power to be masters of ships going to and fro on those waters, the government are carrying their power to an extent which is not usual, and which I should assume very few men would seek to exercise.
